marketing-authorisation.definition: The licence a medicine needs before it may be sold. A regulator gives it only after checking the medicine's quality, its effects and its risks.

medicines-regulator.definition: A government body that decides whether a medicine may be sold, and keeps watching its safety afterwards. Examples are the EMA in the EU, the CBG in the Netherlands and the FDA in the US.

ema.definition: The European Medicines Agency. It checks medicines for the whole EU and advises whether they should be approved.

cbg.definition: The Dutch Medicines Evaluation Board. It decides which medicines may be sold in the Netherlands, and works with the EMA on EU decisions.

fda.definition: The US Food and Drug Administration: the government body that decides which medicines may be sold in the United States.

igj.definition: The Dutch Health and Youth Care Inspectorate. It checks that care and medicines follow the law, and can act against people who sell medicines illegally.

lareb.definition: The Dutch centre that collects reports of side effects. Anyone can report a side effect to Lareb, also for a product bought online.

zorginstituut.definition: The Dutch body that advises which care and medicines basic health insurance should pay for.

wada.definition: The World Anti-Doping Agency. Each year it publishes the list of substances that are banned in sport.

dopingautoriteit.definition: The Dutch national anti-doping organisation. It tests athletes, and gives information about the health effects of doping.

anabolic-steroids.definition: Man-made versions of the male hormone testosterone and related substances, used to build muscle. They are banned in sport.

prescription-only-medicine.definition: A medicine you can only get with a doctor's prescription, from a pharmacy. In the Netherlands, a pharmacist may not hand it over without one.

off-label.definition: Using an approved medicine for something it was not approved for. In the Netherlands a doctor may do this only if professional guidelines exist for that use. While they are still being written, the doctor must first talk it through with the pharmacist.

named-patient-route.definition: A narrow exception that lets one patient get a medicine that has no licence in the Netherlands. The doctor must state that approved medicines cannot be used, and the inspectorate (IGJ) must agree.

clinical-trial.definition: A planned study in people that tests whether a treatment works and what harm it does. Large trials compare it with a dummy treatment or another medicine.

randomised-controlled-trial.definition: A trial in which chance decides who gets the treatment and who gets a comparison, such as a dummy treatment. This makes it a fair test of whether the treatment itself causes the effect.

preclinical-research.definition: Research done in cells and animals before a substance is tested in people. It can show a reason to test something, but not that it works in people.

evidence-profile.definition: This site's four separate grades for each compound: testing in people, the amount of lab and animal research, how independent that research is, and what is known about harms in people.

research-chemical.definition: A label sellers put on products such as peptide vials. It does not make a product a licensed medicine, and it does not mean anyone checked that it is fit to inject.

harm-reduction.definition: Helping people who use a substance anyway to lower the damage it can do, without judging them. Examples are clean needles and clear information about warning signs.

wgbo.definition: The Dutch law on medical treatment, part of the Civil Code. It sets out your rights as a patient: information, consent, privacy and access to your medical file.

informed-consent.definition: Agreeing to a treatment after your doctor has explained what it is for, its risks, and the other options. Without your consent, nothing may be done to you.

medical-file.definition: The record your doctor keeps about your health and treatment. In the Netherlands it is private, and you can ask to see it and get a copy.

second-opinion.definition: A check of your diagnosis or treatment plan by a second, independent doctor in the same field. In the Netherlands your doctor should normally refer you for one if you ask.

knmg.definition: The Royal Dutch Medical Association, the professional body for doctors in the Netherlands. It publishes guidance on how doctors should act.

enema.definition: A liquid that is put into the lower bowel through the anus. Some medicines for bowel disease are given this way.

wet-big.definition: The Dutch law on health care professions. It says who may use titles such as doctor or nurse, and who may do risky procedures such as injections.

reserved-procedure.definition: A medical procedure, such as giving an injection, that Dutch law reserves for doctors and some other care professionals. Others may do it at work only on their instructions.

nhg.definition: The Dutch College of General Practitioners. It writes the guidelines Dutch GPs work by, and runs the patient website Thuisarts.
